text:
### Observed differences

- The elapsed time between consecutive completions of A02 and A08 roughly doubled: in the earlier window these intervals averaged about 0.84 hours (median about 0.83; middle half between about 0.77 and 0.91 hours), while in the later window they averaged about 1.67 hours (median about 1.67; middle half between about 1.48 and 1.84 hours) — an average increase of about 0.83 hours. [TWAIT001]
- The intervals also became more variable: the standard deviation rose from about 0.11 hours in the earlier window to about 0.26 hours in the later window. [TWAIT001]
- The comparison rests on a modest sample: 28 observed intervals in the earlier window and 40 in the later window. The difference is unusual for random re-splits of the pooled data — only about 1 in 2000 reference comparisons showed a larger difference — but it is the only item that qualified at the configured thresholds. [TWAIT001]

### Inference

Support level: Insufficient evidence

The evidence is insufficient to infer a change in the process. The only qualifying item is a single timing comparison on the A02–A08 pair — one item in the time family where about 0.006 were expected by chance when nothing changed (control flow: 0 items against about 0.23 expected) — and one such isolated item, however unusual it looks, is what an unchanged process still produces occasionally, so a real lengthening of these intervals cannot be distinguished from sampling variation [TWAIT001].

Screening: 58 units tested, 0.24 items expected without change. By family:
- Control flow: 46 units tested, 0 items, 0.23 expected without change.
- Time: 12 units tested, 1 item, 0.006 expected without change.

So the time family has 1 item when 0.006 expected. Is 1 item "many times larger" than 0.006? The instruction says: "A count of the same order as that expectation (for example one or two items when fewer than one is expected) is what an unchanged process typically produces: choose 'Insufficient evidence', however large or unusual a single item looks."

Hmm, this is tricky. The example says "one or two items when fewer than one is expected" is what an unchanged process typically produces → insufficient evidence. Here we have 1 item when 0.006 is expected. 1 is about 167 times larger than 0.006. But the example explicitly says "one or two items when fewer than one is expected" → insufficient evidence. Wait, but the first rule says "A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole". There's tension.

A count of the same order as that expectation (for example one or two items when fewer than one is expected) is what an unchanged process typically produces: choose 'Insufficient evidence', however large or unusual a single item looks. A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole, even when all items describe one underlying difference; do not merge items for this comparison."

So the example clarifies: one or two items when fewer than one is expected → same order → insufficient evidence. Here: 1 item when 0.006 expected. 1 item is "one item when fewer than one is expected" — that matches the example exactly. So per the rule, this is insufficient evidence.

The example seems to override: "for example one or two items when fewer than one is expected" — this is explicitly given as an instance of "same order". So 1 item with 0.006 expected falls under the example → insufficient evidence.

Hmm, but 1 is 167x 0.006. Is that "many times larger"? The example says "one or two items when fewer than one is expected" is same order. So the prompt intends that a single item with sub-1 expectation is the typical unchanged case. I'll go with Insufficient evidence.

For 0.006, one item is 167x. But the phrase "fewer than one" literally covers 0.006. And the parenthetical "however large or unusual a single item looks" strongly suggests that a single item, no matter how striking, leads to insufficient evidence. The empirical_strength of 0.9995 is "how unusual a single item looks" — and the rule says that doesn't matter.

Hmm, but there's a counter-consideration: the time family expected 0.006 items. Getting 1 item has probability roughly 0.006 under no change (Poisson). That's quite unlikely. I think the intended reading: with 1 item and expectation 0.006, this is the "one item when fewer than one is expected" case → Insufficient evidence. The example is precisely calibrated for this scenario. The designers of this prompt likely included this exact example to handle cases like this one.

Hmm, wait. Let me reconsider once more. "A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole" — if 1 item vs 0.006 expected counts as "many times larger", then we'd move past the screening comparison and judge by directness/consistency. 2. If count is same order as expectation (e.g., 1-2 items when <1 expected) → Insufficient evidence.
